1.pericope_label: Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness... wash me throughly from mine iniquity

schools.summary: Weigh the title and the vocabulary: Delitzsch defends the ascription, turning the Hebrew's carelessness into evidence, and calls the psalm 'the first of the Davidic Elohim-Psalms'; Ellicott derives blot out from erasing a written record, reads transgression as 'a wilful throwing off of authority or restraint', and alone separates wash (to tread, as clothes are trampled) from cleanse (the priest's formal declaration in leprosy); Delitzsch also defines true penitence as 'a living sensitive consciousness' of sin, no merit but the necessary condition.

Calvin reconstructs the psalm's occasion — David sunk 'into a spiritual lethargy' until roused by Nathan, then anxious to 'testify his repentance to all around him, and leave some lasting proof of it to posterity'; Gill notes that David, under sense of sin, 'does not run away from God, but applies unto him', and reads the intensive washing from the sin's long habitation.

Clarke reports at length the objection that the title cannot stand, verses 4 and 18 both telling against it, and renders the intensive 'wash me again and again... My stain is deep; ordinary purgation will not be sufficient.'

Henry calls the sin 'the inlet to all the other sins that followed... as the letting forth of water' and marks the nine months of silence before repentance; Spurgeon fixes on the order of the words — 'he appeals at once to the mercy of God, even before he mentions his sin' — since 'the sight of mercy is good for eyes sore with penitential weeping'.

positions.view: Reports the objection that verses 4 and 18 rule it out — verse 4 'ill suits the case of David, who laid a successful plot against Uriah's life'.
Defends it, and finds corroboration in the very awkwardness of the Hebrew phrasing.
Take the occasion as given and build the whole reading on it.

debates.question: What do the two verbs of v.2 mean?

positions.view: Both intensive — repeated, thorough washing for a deep stain.
Not merely antithetic: actual purification (treading, as clothes are washed) and ceremonial declaration (the priest in leprosy).

outliers.view: The only voice to make the sequence of the opening words — mercy named before sin — the point of the verse.

themes: Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.
Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.

3.pericope_label: Against thee, thee only, have I sinned... behold, I was shapen in iniquity... thou desirest truth in the inward parts

schools.summary: Ellicott presses the corporate reading hardest here, holding that 'against thee, thee only' 'can refer to nothing but a breach of the covenant-relation by the nation at large', reporting the rabbinic legend that David was born in adultery, and conceding that the argument for a personal author 'seems strong' at v.5 before offering the community as the mother who conceived in sin; Delitzsch states the doctrine plainly, that 'David here confesses his hereditary sin as the root of his actual sin'.

Gill dissolves the difficulty of 'against thee only' by making all sin a transgression against the lawgiver, and guards original sin at both ends — no parental iniquity, no infusion by the Maker, 'seeing God cannot be the author of sin'.

Clarke grants that the Bathsheba affair was 'a public sin... against society at large' and saves the title from David's royal office, then affirms original sin against Grotius by name; Wesley makes 'against thee only' comparative and turns v.5 into a figure — 'this filthy stream leads me to a corrupt fountain'.

debates.question: How can David say he sinned against God only?

positions.view: Comparatively: 'nothing is more grievous to me, than that I have sinned against thee.'
The objection is real; the title survives only because a king 'was not liable to be called to account by any of his subjects'.
It cannot be an individual speaking at all — only the nation, whose sin is a covenant breach.
All sin, however committed, 'is against the lawgiver'.
Yes — Clarke explicitly 'notwithstanding all that Grotius and others have said to the contrary'.
It states hereditary corruption as a truth of experience, but may equally be the community speaking of 'its far-back idolatrous ancestry'.

outliers.view: Alone in reading the whole psalm as the voice of the exiled nation rather than of David.

themes: For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.

7.pericope_label: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean... make me to hear joy and gladness... hide thy face from my sins

schools.summary: Ellicott ties hyssop to the priestly ordinances but subordinates the ritual to the covenant breach, reads the broken bones as sin felt 'to its very fibres', and notes that the hidden face here is 'thy angry look', the reverse of the usual idiom; Delitzsch marks the structural turn, 'the prayer for justification is followed by the prayer for renewing', and defines the clean heart and the stedfast spirit.

Gill lists the three rites hyssop belongs to and draws the self-portrait from them, then distinguishes what sin can and cannot take away — God's favour 'cannot be lost, yet his sensible presence... may'.

Clarke describes the leper's rite in full and observes that it was performed only after healing, 'to declare to the people that the man was healed'; Wesley makes the typology explicit, the blood of Christ 'signified by those ceremonial usages'.

Henry reads the petition as pardon known and privileges restored, and lays down the rule governing his whole reading: these petitions, 'if we do but add, for Christ's sake, are as evangelical as any other'.

debates.question: What does the hyssop imagery establish?

positions.view: That the rite declared a cure already wrought — it 'was not performed till the plague of the leprosy had been healed in the leper'.
Little in itself: 'generally it is a repetition of the former prayer to have the breach made in the covenant-relationship healed'.
A type of the blood of Christ and of the psalmist's own defilement.

debates.question: What has sin taken from him?

positions.view: Not God's favour or his justification, but the sensible presence and the comfortable perception of them.
The testimony of reconciliation, to be sealed again on the conscience by the Spirit.

outliers.view: The only voice to notice that the leper's cleansing rite followed the cure rather than causing it.

themes: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Make me to hear joy and gladness; that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice.
Hide thy face from my sins, and blot out all mine iniquities.

10.pericope_label: Create in me a clean heart, O God... take not thy holy spirit from me... O Lord, open thou my lips

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers 'constant' for right and 'willing' for free, records without joining the Calvinist-Lutheran controversy over 'thy holy spirit', notes that the casting-away phrase elsewhere describes God's formal rejection of Israel, and alone proposes reading 'from death' for 'bloodguiltiness'; Delitzsch rules against the old princely rendering, the word having 'without any doubt, its ethical sense in this passage', and refuses to soften the word for blood-guilt.

Gill argues the new heart from incapacity, the work requiring 'creating power', and distinguishes the salvation that 'can never fail' from the joy of it that may be lost; he takes the bloodguiltiness of the threatened slaughter in David's family.

Clarke insists that 'mending will not avail... it must be new made', makes the Spirit's stay the hinge of hope, and calls the plea for restored joy 'an awful prayer' because it shows the joy had once been had and lost; Wesley renders the spirits 'firm or constant' and 'ingenuous, or liberal, or princely'.

Henry names the crime as murder and strips away the excuse that David 'did not kill him himself'; Spurgeon turns the vow to teach into a doctrine of ministry — 'reclaimed poachers make the best gamekeepers'.

debates.question: What is the 'free spirit' of v.12?

positions.view: A princely, generous spirit, set against a servile one.
Not princely: the word 'has, however, without any doubt, its ethical sense in this passage'.
'Rather, with a willing spirit' — or else 'a willing spirit shall support me'.
Uriah's blood, the phrase that 'gives most color to the propriety of the title'.
The slaughter threatened against David's own house.
Textually uncertain: 'probably we should read from death'.

outliers.view: Alone in reading v.13 as a qualification for ministry rather than a vow of gratitude.

themes: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.
Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.
Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee.
Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.
O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.

16.pericope_label: Thou desirest not sacrifice... the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit... build thou the walls of Jerusalem

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the refusal of sacrifice as fitting a nation deprived of the legal rites rather than an individual, records that an early father long ago referred the last two verses to the Babylonian exiles, and answers the resulting doubt by extending the exilic reading to the whole psalm; Delitzsch supplies the structural reason for the return to material sacrifice, David's prayer for himself passing over into prayer for the city.

Gill notes that the law appointed no sacrifice for murder and adultery, takes the broken spirit evangelically rather than legally, and reports two Jewish views of the closing verses without adopting either.

Clarke supplies the conditional — had such sacrifices been appointed, 'I would cheerfully have given them to thee' — glosses the Hebrew for breaking as our word shiver, and judges the last two verses 'long posterior to the times of David'; Wesley takes the closing prayer at face value, that the temple be built 'notwithstanding my sins'.

Henry states why no offering can serve — the penitent 'cannot make satisfaction for sin' — and adds the qualification the psalm does not supply: 'the broken heart is acceptable to God only through Jesus Christ; there is no true repentance without faith in him.'

positions.view: No: they 'most evidently refer to the time of the captivity... and, consequently, are long posterior to the times of David'.
They are exilic, but so is the whole psalm; the contradiction about sacrifice 'is only apparent'.
Reports both the addition theory and the prophetic one, adopting neither.
Takes them as David's own prayer, unqualified.

debates.question: Why does God refuse sacrifice here?

positions.view: Because the law appointed none for murder and adultery — a statement about David's particular crimes, not about sacrifice as such.
Because a nation cut off from the rites was 'compelled to look beyond their outward form to their inner spirit'.

outliers.view: The only voice to insist that the broken heart is acceptable 'only through Jesus Christ', supplying what the psalm leaves unsaid.

themes: For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
Do good in thy good pleasure unto Zion: build thou the walls of Jerusalem.
Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering: then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar.
